source.title: On the Emergence of Implicit Curriculum in RLVR Learning Dynamics
source.authors: Yu Huang; Zixin Wen; Yue-Jie Chi; Yu-Ting Wei; Aarti Singh; Ying-Bin Liang; Yu-Xin Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some mathematical notation is flattened or garbled in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It tests grokking-like delayed progress in a new setting: mixed-difficulty RLVR on synthetic compositional tasks and multiplication tasks with real language models, rather than supervised grokking on small algorithmic datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper reports reward trajectories across difficulty levels and a theoretical mechanism for delayed handoffs. It does not report the original claim’s training-accuracy saturation followed by test-accuracy growth, or a sweep showing that shrinking the training set increases the delay. Single-length multiplication results are not included as rows because they do not report delayed generalization after a plateau.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows 'grokking' as an analogy for plateau-then-jump reward curves in mixed-difficulty RLVR. No version is tested. The delayed quantity is the training reward on a harder horizon or digit length, which is itself near zero during the plateau. Held-out problems come from the same distribution as training problems. So there is no training-accuracy saturation followed by delayed generalization on the same task, and no memorizing phase. That is a related but different construct: delayed learnability of harder subtasks under sparse reward, not delayed generalization beyond overfitting. There is also no training-set-size sweep, no weight decay, no non-algorithmic data and no optimizer or numerics controls. The theory's hidden progress in the attention score q is a progress account for this different construct, not a generalizing circuit replacing memorization. These findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that outcome-reward RL learns compositions up to a critical horizon, beyond which the gradient is exponentially flat, while SFT is not limited this way. Mixed-difficulty training yields an implicit easy-to-hard curriculum: smooth spectra give relay progress, large gaps give grokking-like plateaus and abrupt transitions. Synthetic and Qwen multiplication runs are offered as corroboration.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses terminal-reward RL (REINFORCE theoretically; GRPO for real-model runs) on mixed-horizon compositional reasoning and multiplication. It does not reproduce supervised grokking on small algorithmic datasets or the original mechanistic-interpretability measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported dynamics vary with the difficulty ratio/gap between training horizons, the task horizon/digit length, and the model/task setting. Moderate-ratio mixtures show relay or staircase progress; larger-gap mixtures can leave the hardest task at zero for the full run.

fits_no_version.finding: In mixed-difficulty RLVR, a large difficulty ratio gives long near-zero-reward plateaus on the next harder horizon, then rapid mastery. A moderate ratio gives shorter, overlapping relay progress. Shown in theory (Theorems 5.1/5.2), a synthetic Z96 task (R=7 vs R=3) and Qwen multiplication mixtures (large gap delays or blocks the hardest digit).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like plateau-then-jump in sparse-reward RL: the delay in learning a harder subtask grows with its difficulty gap from the tasks already mastered.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: during the plateau, gradients from easier horizons keep raising the attention score q (hidden feature sharpening). The harder horizon's reward appears only once q crosses a critical threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hidden continuous progress, driven by easier subtasks, underlies abrupt reward jumps in curriculum-free RL.

record.problems: The empirical results are mostly described from figures without numeric values or uncertainty estimates. Real-model runs have a 1000-update budget and held-out evaluations of 200 problems per digit length. The paper does not report training accuracy alongside held-out accuracy, vary training-set size, or test whether optimizer/numerical choices account for the delays. The real-model multiplication setting is controlled and does not establish the behavior on realistic general-purpose training data.
record.rows_left_out: Single-N multiplication results in Section 7.2/Figure 5 were left out: they report learning limits and transfer, but not delayed plateau-then-rise behavior. Figure 3 fixed-length synthetic results were also left out because the reported near-flat long-horizon reward and attention do not show the mixed-difficulty delayed handoff or a continuous progress measure that anticipates it.

untested.parts: Train-vs-test gap after training accuracy saturates, chance-to-near-perfect test jump, and dependence of the delay on training-set size: none are measured.
No generalizing circuit or memorization removal; the progress measure is theoretical and not an empirical anticipation of a generalization jump.
No non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Real-model runs are RL on synthetic multiplication, not realistic pretraining or fine-tuning data, and do not measure delayed generalization.
No weight decay, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' classification and its V1/V2 labels are withdrawn. 'Grokking' here means a plateau in training reward on a harder subtask, not delayed generalization after memorization. Empirical results are figure-only, with no uncertainty estimates, and real-model runs use a 1000-step budget. The synthetic experiments use an abelian cyclic group even though the theory assumes a non-abelian simple group.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training accuracy saturating while held-out accuracy stays at chance, nor compare training-set sizes to test whether smaller sets require more optimization. The real-model runs cover a finite 1000-step budget.

Analyzes gradual attention-score/feature progress underlying delayed handoffs, but does not identify a Fourier algorithm or show memorizing components being removed. The empirical attention-alignment measurement is from fixed-length synthetic training, not the mixed-difficulty plateau.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule training data; no initialization-scale or weight-norm sweep.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic general-purpose data; multiplication is a controlled reasoning task.
Does not test weight decay, low-norm preference, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
Does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts, or control those factors to assess whether grokking-like delays disappear.

rows.subject: minimal one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: one attention layer and one-hidden-layer MLP; dimensions depend on d
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of length-normalized REINFORCE on a mixed-horizon objective with a large difficulty ratio.
rows.measure: Per-horizon reward over optimization; interval from mastery of one horizon to visible return on the next, then to mastery.
rows.value: Theorem 5.1 states that transitions include a long near-zero-return plateau, followed by rapid progress to mastery after return becomes visible; Tvis,k+1−Tmas,k = Θ(ẽ Lmax·d^(CB−1)/η), and Tmas,k+1−Tvis,k+1 ≤ O(ẽ Lmax·Lk+1/η).
rows.note: A theoretical result about RLVR rewards across task horizons, not supervised train-versus-test accuracy.
rows.check: Theorem 5.1 is a theoretical bound on per-horizon training reward under mixed-horizon REINFORCE, not a measurement. The plateau is a stretch of near-zero training reward on the next horizon, not test accuracy lagging saturated training accuracy. Does not measure V1's construct.

rows.subject: minimal one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: one attention layer and one-hidden-layer MLP; dimensions depend on d
rows.operation_detail: Tracks the theoretical attention parameter q and its gradient contributions during mixed-horizon training.
rows.measure: Progress in q/attention concentration and relative gradients from easier and harder horizons.
rows.value: The analysis states that shorter-horizon updates continue sharpening features while the next horizon’s reward remains near zero; the handoff occurs after a prolonged plateau, when the harder horizon becomes learnable.
rows.locator: Sections 5.2 and 6.2; Lemma 6.2 and Section D.1
rows.note: This is a theoretical progress account; it does not establish Fourier-circuit formation or removal of memorizing components.
rows.check: Theoretical account: attention parameter q keeps sharpening via easier horizons during the plateau (Lemma 6.2, Section D.1). There is no memorizing component and no empirical progress measure. It is analogous to V2 but a different construct.

rows.subject: minimal one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: one attention layer and one-hidden-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical analysis of length-normalized REINFORCE on a mixed-horizon objective with a moderate difficulty ratio.
rows.measure: Per-horizon reward progression and inter-horizon plateau length.
rows.value: Theorem 5.2 gives a shorter inter-horizon plateau than in the large-ratio regime and rapid mastery after visible return; it characterizes overlapping relay progress rather than a long plateau-and-jump sequence.
rows.note: Theoretical RLVR result; the moderate-ratio regime is characterized as smooth relay, not the delayed jump described in V1.
rows.check: Theorem 5.2 is a theoretical relay regime with shorter plateaus. It describes RL training-reward dynamics, not delayed generalization. The V2 link in the record is also unsupported.

rows.subject: cyclic-group synthetic transformer
rows.operation_detail: REINFORCE training on a mixture of reasoning lengths.
rows.measure: Per-length average success rate during training.
rows.value: The text reports a smooth relay across horizons and shortened plateaus between consecutive horizons.
rows.note: The text describes the trend but gives no numeric values for this curve.
rows.check: Synthetic R=3 run, training success per length. Values are figure-only. Note the group is cyclic (abelian), unlike the theory's non-abelian assumption. Not a train-vs-test grokking measure.

rows.subject: cyclic-group synthetic transformer
rows.operation_detail: REINFORCE training on a mixture of reasoning lengths.
rows.measure: Success rate at the longer horizon during training.
rows.value: The longer horizon L=35 remains at near-zero reward throughout training.
rows.note: The finite experimental run shows no later rise for L=35.
rows.check: R=7 run: L=35 stays near zero throughout training. This is a training-reward plateau with no later jump observed. Not V1's construct.

rows.operation_detail: GRPO training on mixed digit-length multiplication prompts.

conditions.value: held-out split; 200 problems per digit length

rows.measure: Held-out per-digit pass@1 over training steps.
rows.value: The smooth-gap mixture produces an easy-to-hard staircase; successive training digits emerge, and the hardest training digit climbs to non-trivial accuracy.
rows.locator: Section 7.2, Figure 1 and Results for mixed-N training
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative pattern but no numerical pass@1 values. It does not say the hardest digit reaches near-perfect accuracy.
rows.check: Held-out pass@1 on training digit lengths drawn from the same distribution, so it tracks learning rather than generalization beyond overfitting. Figure-only; no numbers.
